profile.name: CHRISTIAN PAINCHAUD
profile.headline: Senior Product Manager and entrepreneur
profile.summary: Senior Product Manager and entrepreneur with a strong track record of leading 0→1 SaaS products from ambiguous problem spaces to revenue-generating platforms. Known for structuring complex systems, aligning teams, and driving execution from discovery through delivery. Hands-on with APIs, integrations, and AI tools, using direct building experience to design better products and reduce system complexity.

events.title: Started new role
events.what: Started new role
events.how: I started talking about the idea with players around me. The idea seemed to have traction, it generated enthusiasm. I recruited a co-founder.
events.why: As an ultimate player myself, I sensed an opportunity. My teammates ordered often custom game jerseys from small niche brands. Prices were high, delivery was slow, there were many mistakes and errors in the orders. I figured that it was certainly possible to do much better. I figured that my expertise for mass customization (from Kickflip) would be a great asset in this adventure.
events.outcomes: Taiga Ultimate was founded

events.title: Market research about Ultimate Frisbee: market size, competitors, key regions, key stake holders
events.what: Market research about Ultimate Frisbee: market size, competitors, key regions, key stake holders
events.how: Searched mostly the web, and reached out to people in governing bodies of the sport. I was myself a competitive ultimate frisbee player so I had an extended network already
events.why: I needed to figure the size of the market, the players purchasaing habits, purchasing power. Those assumptions were important to my "starting" business model.
events.outcomes: I made a spreadsheet model of Taiga Ultimate potential revenues and costs - a general first idea, that would set direction, expectations, and set some early targets.

events.title: After closing a first team order I set out to find an apparel distributor and custom printing.
events.what: After closing a first team order I set out to find an apparel distributor and custom printing.
events.how: I focused on local suppliers. I looked online, in the phone book. I called and asked for speed and a good price.
events.why: My knowledge of the apparel industry was null. I had to be able to go fast, and meet the suppliers in person on any day. I knew I had a lot to learn
events.outcomes: I found a first supplier to fulfill the order. I liked the experience and figured I'd start there for the next orders, and shop for other suppliers if they could not deliver.

events.title: I set out to make a first sale of custom team uniforms for an ultimate frisbee team.
events.what: I set out to make a first sale of custom team uniforms for an ultimate frisbee team.
events.how: At games I played, I walked the pitch to meet up with other teams captains. I gave them a frisbee disc in exchange for a 5-10 minutes interview about their sport apparel needs, and what they wish existing brands were doing better. Then I offered to do their next order for them.
events.outcomes: I closed a first team order for 12 custom jerseys at $350 total. And built and early order pipeline for more.

events.title: Built an Ecommerce Website
events.what: Built an Ecommerce Website
events.how: I used Shopify to deploy a website showing the brand and offering team bundles.
events.why: Taiga's competitors biggest weakness was their ordering process. I was complicated, full of friction, and they offered poor online experiences. I had the insight that ordering online seamlessly would be Taiga's competitive advantage.
events.outcomes: I learned how to launch a Shopify store. I learned how to build a brand image.

events.title: Built a sales pipeline
events.what: Built a sales pipeline
events.how: After 2 months of in person hustle at league games and tournaments, orders started to inbound by email.
events.why: Deal flow was critical for Taiga. The company was fully bootstraped. The custom nature of the product made money flow upfront and suppliers paid 45 days later. Thus we could finance growth organically.

events.title: Secured a first tournament sponsorship.
events.what: Secured a first tournament sponsorship.
events.how: Answered RFPs for tournament branded items. For distribution and sales on site.
events.why: This was another good opportunity to increase Taiga's visibility in the local market, and a proof that we could sell our product and services to larger organizations.
events.outcomes: Great opportunity for visibility in the province, in a 1000 persons tournament (100+ teams). But many lessons learned the hard way around processes - production quality, sales and contracts negociations, keeping things simple and really listen to customers needs.

events.title: Created a full product line
events.what: Created a full product line
events.how: Hired apparel designer. Secured manufacturing contract with existing suppliers. Updated Taiga's website to promote this new offer. Made samples to go sell to customers. Sold a first team order for the new product line.
events.why: Based on 6 months of customer feedback we decided to produce and sell our own proprietary products instead of selling only custom printing services. Customers wanted to buy ultimate frisbee specific apparel - designed by and for ultimate players. Competitors were also doing it. So I decided to go head to head in the fight.

events.title: Delivered the first large order of Taiga products to local competitive club.
events.what: Delivered the first large order of Taiga products to local competitive club.
events.how: We made a demo of our new line of products, made locally in Montreal, to local competitive clubs.
events.why: Taiga's full line of products gave us full control over the value chain. Giving us the ability to meet customers needs exactly, and to evolve with no third-party product restrictions. That also placed Taiga in direct competition with the legacy brands.

events.title: Programmed a Adobe Illustrator Automation Script
events.what: Programmed a Adobe Illustrator Automation Script
events.how: Adobe Illustrator has a Macro feature that can handle Javascript scripts. After finding the documentation for this I started coding a solution that automated the customization of jersey printing templates.
events.why: Sublimation printing files are vector files made in Adobe Illustrator. It's basically full size jersey patterns with logos and colors. Each piece of sublimation printing (shorts, jerseys) are represented in the files, and each piece is a unique combo of player's name, number, size, gender, etc. Customizing each item in a team order took hours. Suppliers were charging a heavy fee for this service that was hitting our margins hard. Thus I needed to create my own solution for it.
events.outcomes: After the script was implemented in our production orders workflow, we transformed a 3 hours job in a 10 minutes job and nearly eliminated manual errors. That script took a few weeks of work, but saved tens of thousands of dollars. It also cut the time to production by days. Actually increasing production capacity and thus revenue velocity which is another hundreds of thousands of dollars in value

events.title: Launched e-mail marketing campaings
events.what: Launched e-mail marketing campaings
events.how: Used Mailchimp in the first iteration.
events.why: The customer base had grown to a few thousand persons, we realized that team purchses were actually recurring. We thus set out to add an email marketing layer to the sales engine that preceded the different seasons with tailored value propositions for the players, and team captains. Customer retention and recurring revenue were now key metrics in our business model.
events.outcomes: Lifetime customer value increased by 100%

events.title: Expanded Taiga product line
events.what: Expanded Taiga product line

events.outcomes: Average order size by team and by player increased by 30%

He also had deep connections in the ultimate frisbee world (being a well known elite player) and his skill set in communication would help us increase our marketing operations to grow sales. He was coming from the USA and it was now time to grow in the US market.
events.outcomes: within a few days he started closing deals with US teams.

events.title: Taiga 2 Years Company Milestones
events.what: Taiga 2 Years Company Milestones
events.how: Accomplishments after 2 years
events.why: from the initial business model and following refinement, we tracked key metrics to monitor the health of the company
events.outcomes: We doubled revenues twice. We expanded sales to all Canada and some parts of the USA. We sold to amateur teams and competitive teams. We set and maintained a robust local supply chain. We developed, launched and made revenues from a full line of proprietary products. We made email marketing. Built a high performance Shopify store. Established brand recognition in Quebec and US North East.

events.title: Shipped Shopify Collections Automations
events.what: Shipped Shopify Collections Automations
events.how: Coded product page customization with Liquid framework
events.why: So far, Taiga dealt with a mix of online and offline orders. Offline orders used spreadsheets, emails, and a lot of back and forth. There was a lot of manual data input and translation, and contained more errors. Moving all orders on the online store would make the process much smarter. But we needed to improve the purchasing experience to capture individual players details with precision and standard data format.
events.outcomes: We launched the first dedicated teams collections, it allowed for each player to manage and pay their own part of the team order. It removed a heavy burden from team captains (management and financial). It unlocked up-selling and cross-selling, and it accelerated the sales cycle.

events.title: Implemented HUBSPOT
events.what: Implemented HUBSPOT
events.how: Shopped for sales and marketing solutions. Ultimately landing on Hubspot as a top candidate solution
events.why: Taiga's sales and marketing tech stack had become a frankenstein monster of too many parts. With rapid growth we needed bring all those touch points into an integrated solution. In fact, our new insight was that Taiga operated a B2B2C model, where teams were making purchasing decisions as a business, but the end product was in fact acquired and benefiting individual players.
events.outcomes: We increased sales velocity, and customer retention. Hubspot could be directly integrated with Shopify, and now email marketing was directly supporting sales in full sync from ecommerce signals. Customer success was also easier as now each team and captain information was captured in a proper CRM. Implementing hubspot also helped me implement a full B2B sales framework and increased deal conversion rates as we were adopting best practices.

events.title: First sales in Europe
events.what: First sales in Europe
events.how: We directed sales and marketing efforts towards Europe. I travelled there to meet regional ultimnate frisbee governing bodies. We applied to RFPs.
events.why: To continue our growth we increased the size of the addressable market
events.outcomes: We started closing team orders in Europe, in Belgium, England, and France.

events.what: Taiga 4 Years Company Milestones
events.how: Accomplishments after 2 years
events.why: from the initial business model and following refinement, we tracked key metrics to monitor the health of the company
events.outcomes: Sales  in Canada, USA, Europe. Market dominance in Quebec. Direct competition with top legacy ultimate frisbee brands (accomplished and improved in 4 years all what they did in 12). Doubled revenues two more times to $375000. Deployed a new custom sport apparel ordering standard leveraging Shopify and Hubspot.

events.title: Experienced growth pain in Q2 & Q3 2017
events.what: Experienced growth pain in Q2 & Q3 2017
events.how: New problems to solve in product quality, orders fulfillment, and customer success relations
events.why: Taiga grew bigger than our two heads could contain. The bigger volumes were hitting suppliers capacity limit, and just bigger numbers required more processes to maintain the same quality and accuracy standards.
events.outcomes: We set out to find new partners.

events.title: Ended role
events.what: Ended role
events.how: After the merger with BE Ultimate my role was redefined inside the combined organization
events.why: The combined company needed more focused roles and responsibilities.
events.outcomes: I was assigned the mission to leverage technology to maximize the company efficiency across its operations. From marketing to customer success.

events.title: Initiated and negotiated merger with direct competitor BE Ultimate
events.what: Helped originate and negotiate the merger between Taiga and direct competitor BE Ultimate, turning a long-standing competitive dynamic into a shared growth strategy.
events.how: I was introduced to BE Ultimate's CEO by a mutual friend in the ultimate frisbee community. We met in person at Taiga's WeWork office and quickly recognized both the constant overlap in contracts we were competing for and our shared frustration with large legacy brands in the category. Over the following months, we discussed vision, values, and mission, negotiated terms, and ultimately signed the merger agreement. I kept the discussion moving and helped maintain confidence in the deal when my counterpart considered backing out, reinforcing the strategic case that we could achieve more together than separately.
events.why: The merger was a way to stop wasting energy competing head-to-head for similar business and instead combine complementary strengths to build a stronger challenger in the market. Taiga was strong in technology, ecommerce, marketing, and sales. BE Ultimate was strong in processes, production, and sales. We also shared similar values, mission, vision, and a similar data structure, which reduced integration risk.
events.outcomes: The deal created the foundation for the combined company, which later increased revenue, gained market share, improved profitability, and achieved category dominance in Quebec.

roles.title: Co-owner & Director of E-Commerce
roles.summary_derived: Post-merger, my role was to increase the company's profitability by leveraging technology. BE Ultimate became a leading brand in the category.

events.title: Started post-merger role as Co-owner & Director of E-Commerce
events.what: Started my post-merger role as Co-owner and Director of E-Commerce in the combined company, with a mandate to improve profitability through technology, ecommerce, and cross-functional operating efficiency.
events.how: After the merger closed, my responsibilities shifted from founder-level generalism at Taiga to a more focused role inside the combined business. I took ownership across technology, ecommerce, marketing, sales enablement, customer success, and the data flows connecting those functions.
events.why: The merged company needed clearer role definitions so each leader could focus on the areas where they could create the most leverage. My role was designed to use Taiga's strengths in technology, ecommerce, and commercial operations to help the new entity scale efficiently.
events.outcomes: This role set the stage for the post-merger stabilization work, ecommerce consolidation planning, and the later automation initiatives that improved margins, reduced errors, and increased revenue per employee.

events.title: Championed B Corp certification as a long-term brand and operating commitment
events.what: Pushed BE Ultimate to pursue B Corp certification and framed it as a deeper, more durable response to the social and brand expectations emerging at the time.
events.how: During the Black Lives Matter moment, many brands were issuing public solidarity statements. I argued that BE Ultimate should take a broader and more durable approach by committing to the B Corp framework rather than treating the moment as a short-term PR exercise. I made the business case directly to the CEO, who was the key decision-maker because of the financial and legal implications. After approval, I helped evaluate B Corp consultants and worked with marketing to shape the brand messaging.
events.why: I believed B Corp created long-term brand value because it tied the company to concrete social and environmental standards instead of temporary public positioning. It also provided a framework to structure internal processes around impact, which I saw as more substantive than symbolic responses alone.
events.outcomes: BE Ultimate achieved B Corp certification in 2021. The move strengthened brand trust and differentiation, especially because BE Ultimate was the only company in its industry to make that commitment. During the pandemic, the brand continued to build strength while others stagnated, and it emerged in a stronger position when the sport resumed.
metrics: only company in the industry to make that move

events.title: Led post-merger operating alignment and stabilization across sales, ecommerce, production, and post-sales
events.what: Helped stabilize the newly merged company by integrating two previously separate teams and building a shared operating model across sales, ecommerce, marketing, production coordination, and customer success.
events.how: In the first two months after the merger, I focused on change management: keeping communication clear and frequent, tracking issues as they emerged during business-as-usual operations, and helping teammates resolve incompatible processes quickly. I negotiated with the CEO/co-owner to establish a framework for setting goals and tracking success across the new entity. I then aligned marketing, sales, production, and post-sales around standardized buyer personas, objection handling, and a more consistent sales process. That planning phase shaped the next 12 months of execution, including CRM rollout, ecommerce migration planning, and end-to-end order data improvements.
events.why: The merger created immediate operational risk because two teams with different habits, systems, and ways of working had to function as one company without losing revenue or momentum. The goal was to preserve trust, reduce friction, and create a durable operating foundation for growth and profitability.
events.outcomes: In the first year, revenue increased about 15 percent and market share grew by about 10 percent, outperforming what the two businesses would likely have achieved separately. The company achieved category dominance in Quebec, and profitability improved by leveraging BE Ultimate's lower-cost manufacturing platform. I managed 4 people across tech, marketing, sales, and customer success within a 6-person cross-company team.
metrics: 15% revenue growth in the first year
10% market share growth in the first year

events.title: Redesigned team ordering workflow into self-serve commerce and automated production handoff
events.what: Redesigned BE Ultimate's custom team ordering workflow by connecting HubSpot, Shopify, and Google Sheets so buyers could move from sales commitment to player-level ordering and supplier-ready production handoff with minimal internal manual work.
events.how: Built the integration end-to-end myself using Google Apps Script plus HubSpot and Shopify API work. I customized HubSpot deals to reflect the catalog and opportunity details, modified Shopify product pages to capture player-specific customization like name and number, generated dedicated team collections, and automated the creation of production-ready Google Sheets order documents for the manufacturing partner. Sales reps could trigger collection creation from a control spreadsheet, reducing setup time from more than an hour to minutes.
events.why: The prior workflow depended on email coordination, captain-managed spreadsheets, manual retranscription, and internal double-checking across sales and production. That created delays, high error risk, friction for buyers, and unnecessary operational overhead. The goal was to let sales focus on closing commitments, let production focus on supplier quality, and make the ordering experience the best in the market.
events.outcomes: By 2020, the workflow supported about $1M in annual sales and was growing quickly. It became a major sales differentiator because BE Ultimate could credibly pitch the best ordering experience in the market. The automation reduced errors by more than 80 percent, cut team-collection setup from more than an hour to minutes, improved margins by removing BE-side transcription risk, and directly drove roughly 3x higher revenue per employee. Within about two years, competitors started offering a similar purchasing experience.
metrics: setup time reduced from 1 hour+ to minutes

events.outcomes: I made my way to Alterum,

roles.title: Product Lead
roles.summary_derived: Repositioned a technically complex municipal energy simulation product toward a more viable wedge by turning consultant-style outputs into a more interactive decision tool and aligning the product with ESCO-led municipal decarbonization sales and planning workflows.

events.title: Started new role
events.what: Started new role
events.how: I researched clean teach and climate tech Quebec based VC portfolios. I called founders and asked if they needed help with their product strategy and go to market.
events.why: After my kids were born, I decided I would pledge my career to make the world more sustainable.
events.outcomes: I met David Beauvais, CEO of Alterum, we started working together.

events.title: Hired a senior web designer and rebuilt the product in 3 months
events.what: Hired a senior web designer and helped rebuild the product in 3 months around a more usable decarbonization-planning workflow
events.how: The original application was geared toward a highly specialized energy-grid-planning audience. Its vocabulary centered on grid congestion and energy planning rather than decarbonization, and the experience behaved more like tooling for a consulting shop that output reports than something a broader buyer could interact with. The core output was a large Sankey diagram built from Canadian energy-use databases sliced by geography and end use, but the visualization was too dense for most users to interpret or act on at a glance. I helped recruit a senior web designer on a part-time contract and worked with the development team to rebuild the experience so users could unpack the diagram more explicitly, navigate the components, adjust them based on available information, and understand how those changes affected the broader energy and emissions picture.
events.why: The underlying simulation engine could generate in minutes a municipality-level energy and emissions picture that would otherwise take consultants months and cost thousands of dollars, but the product was optimized for the wrong user and the wrong workflow. We needed to turn a static, engineering-centric report experience into a more modular, dynamic, and informative product that could support municipal decarbonization conversations and later fit a commercial wedge with ESCOs.
events.outcomes: Within 3 months, with strong collaboration from the development team, we shipped a substantially rebuilt product that turned dense consultant-style output into a more interactive decision tool. The new version made it easier to unpack energy and emissions dimensions, identify where to focus first, and support a more commercially viable story. We were then able to demo the new product and set up a pilot project with a Montreal-based Energy Service Company.

events.title: Prospected, nurtured, structured, priced, and signed a pilot project with a Montreal-based Energy Service Company
events.what: Found a design-partner ESCO and co-shaped a municipal decarbonization sales offer around Alterum's product outputs
events.how: I found a champion in the ESCO, the VP of Innovation, and collaborated with him to define what success would mean for both companies. We held working sessions to design an offer for municipalities and map it directly to Alterum's product capabilities. Instead of selling directly to municipalities, which had long cycles and were not a viable wedge, we repositioned Alterum as a tool that could help ESCOs accelerate the early stages of their municipal decarbonization sales motion. The product could generate a municipality-level picture of energy use and emissions in minutes, then help the ESCO turn that output into a decarbonization plan and a slide deck embedded in its sales materials. For example, the ESCO could show that 60 percent of a municipality's emissions came from individual cars, estimate that meeting long-term climate targets would require electrifying 10,000 vehicles, and then propose a program involving citizen adoption, charging infrastructure, and grid coordination. That created a bridge from product output to a potential multi-million-dollar implementation contract.
events.why: We needed real market validation and a repeatable commercial wedge. Selling to municipalities directly was too slow and risky. ESCOs already had the relationships, the service delivery model, and the commercial incentive to use Alterum as a consultative hook for broader decarbonization planning work. For the ESCO, success meant opening a new service-line revenue stream. For Alterum, success meant landing a reference customer, proving a repeatable wedge, and accelerating product-market fit.
events.outcomes: Secured a design-partner relationship, set up a pilot with a Montreal-based ESCO, and validated a much stronger market position for the product as a sales-enablement and planning tool rather than a direct municipal software sale. The ESCO was on track to close three municipal offerings using this approach, with the expectation of cutting pre-sales cost by thousands of dollars and reducing time to action by months.
metrics: thousands of dollars saved in pre-sales cost
stakeholders: VP of Innovation at design-partner ESCO

events.title: Ended role
events.what: Ended role
events.how: After a discussion with the founder and CEO, we decided to go separate ways
events.why: Despite my best efforts, I could not convince the CEO to stay committed to the ESCO wedge and the product repositioning. He turned the effort back into an engineering contest, which I believed we were unlikely to win against established engineering firms.
events.outcomes: The ESCO pilot fell apart as the strategic commitment weakened, and the company closed about 10 months later. The experience reinforced how important it is to align product positioning, company strategy, and commercial execution rather than relying only on technical strength.

roles.title: Senior Product Manager
roles.summary_derived: Explored how pre-LLM conversational AI could drive ecommerce revenue rather than only customer-support savings, and shaped internal tooling initiatives to speed script creation, customer onboarding, and product experimentation by moving conversation designers beyond spreadsheet-driven workflows.
roles.notes: Reported to the VP of Product inside a roughly 50-person product and technology organization that included data scientists and AI researchers. There were about 5 PMs total; I was the only PM on my surface and operated with high autonomy, owning initiatives end to end and asking for help when blocked.

events.title: Started as Senior Product Manager
events.what: Started as Senior Product Manager
events.how: I sent a resume, went through interviews, and made a home assignment during the interview process.
events.why: My goal was to work in a solid product team to effectively make the jump from "founder" to product manager. HEyday clients were e-commerce brands, something I was expert of, having owned my own e-commerce brand for several years. Following my experience at Alterum, I knew I needed to perfect the PM craft and needed managers who'd teach, coach, and help me grow professionnally.
events.outcomes: I was hired. My home assignment hit the bulls eye vs their current product vision and strategy. The hiring manager even asked me if I had interviewed people at Heyday for my assignment (i did not). My product vision and insights were outstanding.

events.title: Shaped an internal tooling concept to turn sales-chatbot scripting into a faster, more scalable product workflow
events.what: Explored, validated, and shaped a new product direction for Heyday's ecommerce chatbots: using them to drive sales rather than positioning them mainly as customer-support cost savers. To make that possible, I proposed improving the internal tooling used to create sales scripts so the conversation-design team could iterate faster and eventually let ecommerce managers supply more of their own content.
events.how: This was before ChatGPT and before modern LLM-based chat experiences. At the time, the chatbot logic relied largely on predefined conversation trees, with AI mainly acting as a routing layer that matched user questions to prewritten answers. Three internal conversation designers maintained those flows using complicated spreadsheet templates. Any modification to the spreadsheet required corresponding changes to the parsing logic that translated spreadsheet content into the script format the application actually used, so the spreadsheet-to-software layer became a painful mix of manual work and scripting work. I identified this as a key bottleneck: they were doing essential work, but the tooling made exploration and innovation slow. I interviewed about 10 customers directly, ranging from large enterprise brands like Decathlon to smaller shops like Quilicot Bikes, to understand what sales generation through chat actually meant in their context. The most common use cases were product discovery and guided selling, but the broader opportunity also included upsell, abandoned-cart rescue, and bundle recommendation. I partnered with a UX researcher, a web designer, the conversation-design team, a technical lead, and a front-end developer, and used Confluence, Jira, and Figma to align the concept and track the work. My proposed proof of concept was to replicate the few existing sales scripts inside improved tooling, then modify them and compare the speed of the feedback loop against the traditional spreadsheet-driven workflow.
events.why: If we could improve the script-authoring workflow first, we could unlock two advantages at once: increase the pace of experimentation around sales-generating chatbot experiences, and reposition conversation designers toward a more leveraged "conversation architect" role while moving some content entry closer to the ecommerce managers themselves. I also saw clear business upside in faster onboarding, faster time to value, and lower sales costs. More broadly, I felt the old setup was making us offer a static solution in a problem space that should have been highly creative and fast-moving. For external success, I would have looked at the volume of sales-type conversations in chatbot activity logs and how many of those conversations led to add-to-cart CTA clicks. For internal success, I would have tracked the number of conversations designed per week before and after the tooling change, because with a constant team size that would indicate higher output and should cascade into improvements in onboarding cost and time.
events.outcomes: By the time I was laid off in Hootsuite's restructuring, we were on track to ship a major internal feature and begin testing it. The work sharpened my ability to connect user research, internal workflow bottlenecks, AI constraints, and tooling strategy into one coherent product direction. It also clarified an important change-management lesson for me: some conversation designers initially worried the project might take their jobs away, and I came away feeling I could have done a better job early on explaining how the tooling could upgrade their role rather than replace it. During my first three months at Heyday, I also ramped by following people across the company in meetings, learning the business and customers quickly, and becoming a product subject matter expert on the Heyday domain.

As part of the work, we also introduced clearer affordances for customer users so they could navigate more easily between sandbox and production accounts.

We needed a more standardized and scalable setup path to cut onboarding cost, accelerate time to value, and keep engineering focus on harder work.

events.title: Owned quarterly roadmap updates and a structured initiative-to-PRD delivery process for my product surface
events.what: Managed my surface through a quarterly roadmap and a repeatable operating model for turning ambiguous initiatives into development-ready product work and customer-facing rollout plans.
events.how: Each quarter, I updated a high-level roadmap for my surface in collaboration with the VP of Product. That roadmap was used in sales calls and customer-success QBRs with large accounts, and my progress was tracked against it. Operationally, I created an initial pitch document for each initiative, something close to an initiative overview, and explored it early with a development team lead to surface hidden risks, technical limits, and implementation challenges. Once the initiative was pressure-tested, I split it into self-contained problems to solve and pieces to ship, then turned those into PRDs that could be added to upcoming development cycles based on available resources. During delivery, I partnered with the product marketing person to prepare rollout documentation for the customer success team and for clients. The motion was much more meeting-and-slides based than web- or email-based.
events.why: The work needed a structure that kept strategy, engineering reality, and customer communication connected. A simple roadmap was not enough on its own; we also needed a disciplined way to de-risk initiatives early, scope them into shippable parts, and prepare the organization to support them once released.
events.outcomes: This operating model gave me a practical way to own my surface end to end with high autonomy while staying aligned with leadership, engineering constraints, and the needs of large customer accounts. It strengthened my ability to connect roadmap strategy, technical risk review, PRD quality, and rollout readiness into one coherent product-management motion.

events.title: Shipped an energy modeling improvement called "calibration"
events.what: Shipped an energy modeling improvement called "calibration"
events.how: Partnered with data scientists, building engineers, customer energy managers, and the customer success team to understand energy data flaws. Published data acquisition guidelines for CS managers. Provided guidance to developers on scope.
events.why: Calibration adjusts modeling results to real-world data, giving users a realistic idea of potential energy and carbon savings and budget. It was crucial for proving the credibility of our solution.
events.outcomes: Shipped a first, imperfect version that convinced customer technical teams of our solution's credibility. Learned the importance of building visibility into modeling engines to avoid technical debt and improve troubleshooting.

events.title: Built observability around AI energy-modeling accuracy to overcome technical buyer objections
events.what: Helped the data science team build observability around a neural network trained to replicate traditional energy-modeling software results, with the goal of improving modeling accuracy and expanding the range of building types supported.
events.how: Defined internal dashboard needs for error analysis across parameters such as building type, climate zone, pure inference stage, energy calibration stage, and equipment validation stage. The team compared inferred consumption against actual consumption whenever customer data was available, and relied on trusted synthetic reference data when it was not. I worked across product and technical stakeholders to ensure the outputs were understandable and useful for iteration and sales credibility.
events.why: Technical buyers repeatedly challenged modeling accuracy during the sales process. We needed stronger observability to guide model improvement, reduce skepticism, and make the system commercially credible.
events.outcomes: Helped the team overcome technical objections on prediction accuracy by showing the system could land within about 80% precision in seconds for a few dollars, versus traditional approaches that could take months and thousands of dollars to reach full accuracy. This moved energy audits further down the operating pipeline and contributed to higher pilot conversion once a hidden confidence threshold was reached.

events.title: Reduced the bug backlog by over 50% and stopped its growth

events.why: Bugs and technical debt consumed over 60% of development attention, leading to delayed and expensive features, and impacting company survival.
events.outcomes: Reduced bug backlog by 50% and stopped its growth over 2 years.

events.title: Integrated rooftop HVAC computer vision into the modeling system with confidence guardrails and fallback logic
events.what: Helped shape a rooftop detection system that used aerial HD imagery to identify rooftop boundaries, rooftop HVAC units, gas lines, and equipment types, then fed those results into the energy-modeling system to improve inferred equipment lists.
events.how: Focused on making the detection system connect cleanly with the SaaS platform and improve overall system performance. I helped define guardrails around confidence handling, rejecting low-confidence outputs and falling back to standard inference when detection returned nothing. I also had to stay vigilant because early versions often crashed the modeling layer and the application. Key failure cases included wrong rooftop boundaries, incorrect overlap between rooftop and address, and low-confidence or unreliable detections.
events.why: Existing inference methods based only on localized construction standards and cross-referenced datasets were not accurate enough to support the level of modeling quality we wanted. We needed another signal source to improve confidence in inferred heating, cooling, and ventilation equipment.
events.outcomes: Strengthened the product's demo story and made prospects visibly more confident in the system. While the direct impact on modeling quality was difficult to measure precisely, the feature improved trust in the inferred equipment list and contributed to overcoming technical skepticism during the sales process.

events.title: Designed the data architecture for conversational career discovery
events.what: Built the core data architecture and database foundation that made Elite AI's conversational product experience possible.
events.how: Designed and implemented a Python and FastAPI backend with a PostgreSQL database, server-rendered HTML templates over the wire, and minimal JavaScript. Defined the structured timeline and event model, privacy and visibility defaults, owner-versus-visitor boundaries, session patterns, and the deterministic data shape needed to support both profile building and public discovery.
events.why: The product needed stronger AI grounding and a better public discovery experience than static resumes or loosely structured chat inputs could provide.
events.outcomes: Created a foundation that supported reliable AI grounding, safer database interactions, and a more coherent public experience where visitors could explore professional stories through context-aware conversations.

events.title: Enabled AI agents to interact safely with career data

events.why: These AI features were what made the app feel useful and differentiated, but database writes required guardrails to reduce bad edits or data loss.

events.title: Launched a live MVP of Elite AI
events.what: Built and launched Elite AI, a web app with agentic features that turns a resume into a living conversational profile visitors can explore through chat.
events.how: Built the full application myself using a repeatable loop of agent support: product ideation and framing, narrow PRDs for production-ready features, agentic coding, and human review by me until the MVP reached an acceptable quality bar. Implemented a Python and FastAPI backend with a PostgreSQL database, server-rendered HTML templates over the wire, and minimal JavaScript, then deployed the application on Render. The product included profile creation, conversational discovery, interview-guided profile building, resume import, timeline management, and privacy controls.
events.why: Wanted to create a better alternative to static resumes and generic job platforms by making professional stories more discoverable, interactive, and grounded in actual experience. Also used the project to test how far modern AI tools could accelerate end-to-end product building.

events.title: Implemented PostHog to monitor user behavior in Elite AI
events.what: Implemented PostHog in Elite AI to track whether users completed the intended product flows and to see where they stumbled in the experience.
events.how: Added product analytics instrumentation around key user journeys so I could observe whether the UX happy path was actually happening for people who tried the product and identify friction points that needed attention.
events.why: I needed direct behavioral evidence instead of relying on intuition to understand whether the product experience was working and where users were getting blocked.
events.outcomes: Created a clearer view of user progress and friction inside the product, making it easier to evaluate UX quality and spot where the experience was breaking down.

events.title: Launched Super Capitaine to simplify weekly sports lineup management
events.what: Built Super Capitaine, a focused web app for recreational sports captains to manage weekly game attendance without chasing players across texts, emails, and spreadsheets.
events.how: Built the product from scratch using the AI-assisted product development workflow developed during Elite AI and continued improving it through this project. Implemented a Python and FastAPI backend with a PostgreSQL database, server-rendered HTML templates over the wire, and as little JavaScript as possible. Designed and built the full MVP including account creation, sign-in and sign-out, team creation, game creation, player management, email-driven invitations, and RSVP web flows for confirming player availability.
events.why: The idea came from repeatedly experiencing the same coordination problem across hockey, ultimate frisbee, and soccer teams, as well as while coaching my son's hockey team. I saw that captains were wasting an outsized amount of mental energy every week just figuring out who was playing.
events.outcomes: Launched a live MVP at https://supercapitaine.com and began running pilots with people around me. The product was intentionally scoped to do one thing very well rather than expand into a broader team-management tool.

events.title: Focused the product on core captain UX instead of feature breadth

Deliberately kept the product small and operational, prioritizing the captain journey from roster setup to invitation sending to player confirmation.
events.why: This category is easy to replicate, so the real differentiation was not feature count but nailing the experience captains actually need every week.
events.outcomes: Created a clearer MVP with tighter scope and a more opinionated user experience centered on reducing weekly coordination load for captains.

events.title: Implemented PostHog to monitor user behavior in Super Capitaine
events.what: Implemented PostHog in Super Capitaine to track whether users completed the intended product flows and to see where they stumbled in the experience.
events.how: Instrumented the core captain and player journeys so I could verify whether the UX happy path was happening for real users and identify the points where they were dropping off or getting confused.
events.why: I wanted product decisions to be informed by actual user behavior, especially in a narrowly scoped product where UX quality on the main flow mattered more than feature breadth.
events.outcomes: Made it easier to assess whether the product's core experience was working as intended and where user friction needed to be reduced.
